The work of critical care nurses can be divided into three connected but independent work areas. The first is continuous assessment and monitoring: monitor vital signs and ECG and oxygen saturation and respiration by frequency or continuously, review laboratory and monitoring data, assess pain and sedation needs, observe signals of condition change such as sepsis or shock, verify the values and alarms of equipment such as ventilators and oxygen therapy and pressure monitoring, and record the assessment results. The second is order execution and life support nursing: after verifying orders and patient identity, execute medication and blood transfusion and fluid management by route and per standards, complete airway and line care and specimen collection and approved therapeutic or diagnostic procedures, assist doctors with bronchoscopy and endoscopy and endotracheal intubation or elective cardioversion, and observe adverse reactions. The third is records, handover, and teamwork: complete nursing records and treatment plans and outcome records per standards, use a structured handover to explain the condition and the measures taken and the items to observe to the next shift and the interdisciplinary team, identify equipment failure or nutrition and psychosocial risk and
report promptly, provide explanation and emotional support to patients and families, and take part in nursing standards and quality improvement. The three work areas alternate, but their basis and responsibility and risk differ; the ICU and CCU and post-operative recovery and emergency critical care and neonatal intensive care settings also differ in monitoring intensity and division of work.

Core purpose

Provide continuous specialty registered nursing to critically ill or injured patients: ensure vital signs and monitoring are continuously assessed and orders and life support are accurately executed and condition changes are identified and escalated promptly, with reviewable nursing records.

Core purposes of adjacent positions: registered nurses (parent occupation) cover registered nursing across departments and settings; acute care nurses care for acutely ill or post-surgical patients; licensed practical and vocational nurses provide basic nursing under guidance; nurse practitioners (advanced practice) carry advanced practice duties such as diagnosis and prescribing; nurse anesthetists carry anesthesia and peri-anesthesia nursing. 
US advanced practice diagnosis and prescribing and anesthesia duties depend on state law and license and actual role and may be independent or collaborative, and not all advanced practice nurses are unrestricted and independent; the same-named Chinese positions cannot be directly equated.
Main object and basis

Critically ill or injured patients and monitoring and life support equipment and orders and medications, as well as nursing records and handover information; the basis is nurse practice registration and hospital critical care competency admission and orders and nursing technique standards and patient safety and infection prevention policy.

Objects and bases of adjacent positions: patients across departments and nursing standards (registered nurses), acutely ill or post-surgical patients and acute care standards (acute care nurses), basic nursing tasks and scope of practice (licensed practical and vocational nurses), diagnostic and prescribing authorization (advanced practice), and anesthesia and peri-anesthesia standards (nurse anesthetists).
Core process

Continuous assessment and monitoring → verify orders and patient identity → execute medication and life support nursing → identify anomalies and escalate → record and hand over; and assist with procedures and take part in quality improvement as needed.

US RNs provide registered nursing per the actual department; acute care may include life-threatening conditions and complex monitoring and emergency care; LPNs/LVNs provide basic care within their scope; NP diagnosis and prescribing and CRNA anesthesia tasks depend on state license and role and collaboration conditions, and unrestricted independence for all or cross-jurisdiction interchange is not inferred.
Main outputs
Vital sign and monitoring records, medication and procedure execution records, condition escalation and handover records, patient and family communication records, and quality improvement material.

Outputs of adjacent positions: nursing records by department (registered nurses), acute care records (acute care nurses), basic nursing records (licensed practical and vocational nurses), diagnosis and prescribing records (advanced practice), and anesthesia and peri-anesthesia records (nurse anesthetists).
Responsible party

Nurses in this occupation are responsible for continuous assessment and order execution and monitoring escalation and the truthfulness and completeness of records; whether they can work independently and whether they can perform high-risk techniques must be handled per hospital critical care competency admission and the authorization chain and are not decided unilaterally.

Responsible parties of adjacent positions: registered nurses are responsible for registered nursing in their position; acute care nurses are responsible for acute care; licensed practical and vocational nurses are responsible within their scope of practice; advanced practice nurses are responsible for diagnosis and prescribing; nurse anesthetists are responsible for anesthesia and peri-anesthesia nursing. US advanced practice diagnosis and prescribing and anesthesia duties depend on state law and license and actual role and may be independent or collaborative, and not all advanced practice nurses are unrestricted and independent; the same-named Chinese positions cannot be directly equated.
Collaboration and supervision

Article 17 of China's Nurses Regulation: on discovering a critical condition, notify the physician immediately; for rescuing a dying patient, first carry out the necessary emergency rescue. On discovering that an order violates the rules, raise it with the physician and, if necessary, report it to the department head or the medical service management head. Equipment failure and medication questions and matters beyond authority are verified and help is sought per real ability and matter and hospital standards, and all nursing or rescue cannot be uniformly stopped.

Collaboration of adjacent positions: registered nurses collaborate with the ward team; acute care nurses collaborate with the emergency or ward team; licensed practical and vocational nurses work under the guidance of a registered nurse or physician; advanced practice nurses collaborate with the medical team; nurse anesthetists collaborate with the surgical and anesthesia team.
Conclusion boundary

Similar position titles do not mean the same duties: whether the object is critical care continuous monitoring and life support, general ward nursing, acute care nursing, basic nursing, advanced practice diagnosis and treatment, or anesthesia nursing, and whether the role carries independent assessment and authorization, determines the scope of duties and the assessment method, and cannot be interchanged by name.

The preparation levels and authorization conditions of adjacent positions do not apply to this occupation and must be verified item by item against each occupation's official material and the institution's rules.
Key occupation judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: whether vital signs and monitoring are continuously and accurately assessed; whether orders and patient identity are correctly verified and medication and life support are executed per standards; whether condition changes and equipment alarms are identified and escalated promptly; whether records and handover are truthful and complete and traceable; whether infection prevention and high-risk techniques are performed within the authorized scope; and whether patient safety events or equipment failures or authorization boundary issues are escalated per policy.

Editorial potential risk observation: confirm that vital signs and ECG and respiration are monitored by frequency or continuously, and that laboratory and monitoring data are verified and abnormal trends identified; a missed assessment or delayed identification may affect the timing of rescue.

Editorial potential risk observation: before medication and blood transfusion and fluid management, verify the order and patient identity and dose and route, and observe and record adverse reactions after execution; a verification gap may cause serious consequences such as a medication error.

Editorial potential risk observation: for signals such as sepsis or shock or equipment alarms, assess per procedure and escalate promptly to the medical team; a delayed escalation may delay the intervention window.

The difference is that the object is acutely ill or post-surgical patients with monitoring intensity usually lower than a critical care unit; this occupation serves critically ill or injured patients and carries continuous life support and high-risk techniques.
Better suited to people who want to care for acutely ill or post-surgical patients with relatively manageable monitoring intensity.
Licensed practical and vocational nurses (adjacent occupation, 29-2061.00)

The difference is that the scope of practice and authorization level are lower and they usually do not independently carry critical care monitoring and life support; this occupation requires deeper assessment and execution responsibility.
Better suited to people who want to enter the nursing workforce first and accumulate clinical experience under guidance.
Nurse practitioners (advanced practice) (adjacent occupation, 29-1171.00)

The difference is that it has independent diagnostic and prescribing authorization and usually requires graduate education and advanced practice certification; this occupation does not have independent diagnostic and prescribing authorization.
Better suited to people who are willing to pursue long-term further study and take on diagnostic and prescribing responsibility.
Nurse Anesthetists (adjacent occupation, 29-1151.00)

The difference is that the specialty area is anesthesia and the peri-anesthesia period and usually requires graduate education and certification; this occupation serves continuous life support nursing in critical care units.
Better suited to people who want to carry specialty nursing in surgical and anesthesia settings.
Advanced Practice Psychiatric Nurses (adjacent occupation, 29-1141.02)

The difference is that the object is mental health and it has advanced practice authorization and usually requires graduate education; this occupation serves monitoring and life support for critically ill patients.
Better suited to people interested in mental health care who are willing to pursue further study.

values: Hypothetical critical care scenario material (practice input)

Hypothetical situation: a critical care nurse on a night shift encounters four problems. First, a patient's oxygen saturation and respiratory rate drop markedly between two recordings, and the monitor alarm signals an anomaly; second, the dose in a newly ordered intravenous medication seems not to match the patient's weight; third, an infusion pump repeatedly alarms during operation and prompts for inspection; fourth, the patient's family asks to see another patient's laboratory results and asks about bed arrangements.

Given materials: the hypothetical patient's vital sign and laboratory records and monitoring alarm records; the order and medication list; an excerpt of the equipment manual; and the hospital's policy statement on patient information protection and visiting communication.

Materials not given: the specific handling thresholds and escalation targets for a monitoring anomaly, the discretion rule for which prevails when a dose verification conflicts, the scope of equipment faults that may be handled on your own, and the specific provisions on the shareable scope of patient information. If the practice needs these conditions, state clearly your assumptions and the party you need to confirm them with.
Task requirements

Please write a one-page handling and communication plan: including the assessment and escalation of the monitoring anomaly, the verification and reporting of the medication dose, the handling of and help-seeking for the equipment alarm, and the compliant response to the family information request.

The plan must state which information comes from the prompt material and which is still an assumption, and explain whether it relies on the monitoring records or the order list or the equipment manual or the hospital policy statement.
Reference deliverables (derivable from the prompt)

The plan should include: the monitoring anomaly (confirm the trend against the records, assess at the bedside per procedure and escalate immediately to the medical team, and continue monitoring and recording before confirmation), the medication dose question (pause execution and re-verify the order and weight and dose, confirm with the physician or pharmacist before executing, and record the verification and communication), equipment failure (troubleshoot per the manual and procedure and replace the equipment and report when necessary, handle it without affecting patient safety, and seek help when beyond scope), the family information request (explain that patient information
is protected and is not disclosed to others, and provide an executable communication and visiting channel per hospital policy), and handover (state clearly the status of the four matters and the actions taken and the to-be-confirmed items).
The reference deliverables list only the elements that should be included and do not require wording identical to the example; being able to explain the judgment basis is enough.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be inferred

This question only tests monitoring assessment and order verification and equipment handling and awareness of information protection; it does not evaluate whether handling of a real clinical case is compliant and does not constitute diagnosis and treatment or authorization or disciplinary or legal advice.

Real patient data or un-de-identified personal information must not be used; where real diagnosis and treatment and medication and equipment handling and information sharing are involved, follow hospital policy and applicable rules.

description.text: Critical care nurses (O*NET-SOC 29-1141.03) provide specialty registered nursing to critically ill patients in settings such as intensive care units: this covers continuous assessment of vital signs and laboratory data, administering medication and life support nursing per orders, monitoring equipment such as ventilators and ECG monitors, identifying changes such as sepsis or shock and escalating promptly, collaborating with the interprofessional team to revise treatment plans, completing nursing records and handover, and family communication and quality improvement; it includes the US 2025 parent occupation basis median annual wage of 97,550 US dollars, about 3,391,000 people employed in 2024 (parent occupation Registered Nurses proxy), a 2024—2034 employment projection growth of 5% to 6% (faster than average), about 189,100 average annual openings including growth and replacement, industry employment concentrated in health care and social assistance (84%), the interest code SIC, the Mainland China occupation-level wage and independent specialty license gaps, and the control points of patient identity verification, medication and life support safety, line and equipment management, infection prevention and control, and record responsibility boundaries.

subject.name: Critical care nurses
subject.summary: In the United States critical care nurses correspond to O*NET-SOC 29-1141.03 (Critical Care Nurses) and provide specialty registered nursing to critically ill or injured patients in settings such as intensive care units (ICU/CCU): continuously assess vital signs and laboratory data, administer medication and life support nursing per orders, monitor equipment such as ventilators, ECG monitors, oxygen therapy, and pressure monitoring, identify condition changes such as sepsis or shock and escalate promptly, collaborate with the interprofessional team to develop and revise treatment plans, complete standardized nursing records, handover, and family communication, and take part in quality and process improvement. The preparation level for this occupation is Job Zone Four (most require a four-year bachelor's degree in nursing), and US wage, employment, and industry data are published on O*NET on the parent occupation registered nurse (Registered Nurses) basis; the comparable position on the Chinese side is a registered nurse in hospital critical care medicine departments and intensive care units, where basic practice registration is managed in tiers along with hospital critical care competency admission and high-risk technique authorization, and it cannot be interchanged with the US preparation level.
